I have been farming this land in Quzhou for 45 years, and at 65 years old, I know what my two-person household can handle. My wheat is already in the ground from last autumn—that is my foundation, and I will top-dress it with urea at the green-up stage and irrigate it three times from the well because water is my advantage here. After the wheat comes off in early June, I will immediately plant hybrid maize on those same 10 mu; the soil is good and the timing is tight, so I will rotary-till right after harvest and get the seed in the ground. I keep 2.5 mu of cotton because it brings decent money, but it is back-breaking work with all the pruning and spraying for bollworm, so I cannot plant more than that with just my wife and me. The 2 mu of peanut is easier money and fixes the soil a bit. I always keep a small plot of millet and mung bean—about 0.8 mu each—because the millet porridge and mung bean soup are good for our health, and these crops do not complain if I miss an irrigation. I use improved seeds for wheat, maize, cotton, and peanut because the yield difference is real, but for millet and mung bean I save my own seed; it is cheaper and good enough for home use. I will plough the cotton field deep because cotton likes loose soil, but rotary tillage is enough for everything else. I do not chase the highest possible yield anymore—I aim for steady, reliable harvests that do not break my back or my wallet.
